content: Individuals with sickle cell disease (SCD) are at a significantly increased risk of developing infections caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Before the introduction of Hib conjugate vaccines in high-income countries, this pathogen was a leading cause of death in children under the age of five. In African nations, where vaccination coverage remains alarmingly low, Hib continues to be one of the most frequent causes of bloodstream infections (bacteraemias) in children with SCD. Expanding the use of Hib conjugate vaccines in these regions could greatly enhance survival rates among children with SCD. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate whether Hib conjugate vaccines reduce mortality and morbidity in individuals with SCD. Secondary objectives included assessing the immune response (immunogenicity) elicited by these vaccines, their safety profile, and whether their effectiveness varies based on factors such as vaccine type, method of administration (as a standalone vaccine or combined with others), the number of doses administered, and the age at which the first dose is given. To gather evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases, journal handsearches, and conference abstracts. They also reviewed clinical trial registries and reached out to pharmaceutical companies to identify any unpublished studies. The most recent search of the trials register was conducted on December 18, 2017. The review sought to include all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared Hib conjugate vaccines to either a placebo or no treatment, as well as studies comparing different types of Hib conjugate vaccines in individuals with SCD. However, no trials meeting these criteria were identified. Despite the lack of evidence from RCTs, there has been a marked reduction in invasive Hib infections among individuals with SCD in high-income countries following the introduction of Hib conjugate vaccines. This suggests that these vaccines are likely to be beneficial for children with SCD, particularly in African countries where the disease burden is high. Implementing universal Hib vaccination as part of routine childhood immunization schedules could significantly improve survival rates for children with SCD in low-income settings. Currently, there is insufficient data to determine the potential benefits of Hib vaccination in unvaccinated adults with SCD. Further research is needed to establish the most effective Hib vaccination schedule for both children and adults with SCD.
